summary: Defines a new name form for the otherName field of the X.509 Subject Alternative Name and Issuer Alternative Name extensions so a certificate can be tied to an internationalized email address. It updates RFC 5280 and obsoletes RFC 8398.

eli5.summary: Email addresses can now use many alphabets. This gives certificates a proper place to write such an address.

questions: how to put an internationalized email address in a certificate
subtitle: How a certificate names an email address whose local part is not plain ASCII, and how to compare such names.

tldr.problem: The certificate name type for email addresses, rfc822Name, only allows a subset of US-ASCII, so it cannot hold internationalized email addresses.
tldr.mechanism: A new otherName form, SmtpUTF8Mailbox, carries the address as a UTF8String with the domain written in A-label form, and names are compared octet for octet after a small setup.
tldr.outcome: It obsoletes RFC 8398 and simplifies it by always using A-labels for domains. It also updates RFC 5280.

today: RFC 9598 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 8398 and updates RFC 5280. The metadata lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why a New Name Form
sections.content:
RFC 5280 defines the rfc822Name name type for email addresses in X.509 certificates. Its syntax is restricted to a subset of US-ASCII, so it cannot represent internationalized email addresses.

This document defines a new otherName variant for those addresses. It also requires all email address domains in X.509 certificates to conform to IDNA2008.

It obsoletes RFC 8398. The main motivation is simpler handling of domain labels: RFC 8398 allowed either A-labels or U-labels, and this document mandates A-labels in all cases.
sections.eli5: The old place for an email address on a certificate only understood plain English letters. Now there is a new spot that understands letters from many languages.

sections.title: The SmtpUTF8Mailbox Name Form
sections.content:
The SmtpUTF8Mailbox form lives in otherName, so it can appear in a subjectAltName, an issuerAltName, or anywhere else that GeneralName is used. Its identifier is id-on 9 and its value is a UTF8String of at least one character.

The value follows the internationalized Mailbox syntax of RFC 6531, with refinements. Any domain label containing non-ASCII characters MUST be stored as an A-label, not a U-label. Labels that are ASCII only use NR-LDH restrictions. All such domain labels SHALL be encoded in lowercase so values can be compared octet for octet.

Like rfc822Name, it is an envelope mailbox: no phrase before it, no comment after it, and no angle brackets. The UTF8String MUST NOT contain a Byte Order Mark.
sections.eli5: It is a label that holds the whole email address in a standard way: the part before the @ may use any alphabet, and the website part is always written in a plain-letters code.

sections.title: When to Use Which Form
sections.content:
To stay compatible with legacy software and with name constraints, SmtpUTF8Mailbox MUST NOT be used unless the Local-part of the address contains non-ASCII characters. If the Local-part is ASCII, rfc822Name MUST be used instead, even when the domain has Unicode in it.

A non-ASCII Local-part may also contain ASCII characters.

Separately, all email domains in X.509 certificates, in both SmtpUTF8Mailbox and rfc822Name, MUST conform to IDNA2008 and avoid any mappings.
sections.eli5: If the first half of the address is plain letters, use the old spot. Only use the new spot when the first half has letters from other alphabets.

sections.title: Matching Addresses
sections.content:
Two SmtpUTF8Mailbox values are equivalent only if they match octet for octet. Comparing a SmtpUTF8Mailbox with an rfc822Name always fails, because one has a non-ASCII Local-part and the other is all ASCII.

To compare a certificate value with an address from another source, such as a received message or user input, first remove any phrases, comments and angle brackets. Then convert any U-labels in the domain to A-labels, and lowercase uppercase letters in NR-LDH and A-label labels. The Local-part must conform to RFC 6530 and RFC 6531 and MUST NOT be transformed in any way, such as case folding or normalization. Then compare octet for octet.

No wildcard characters are defined, and implementations MUST NOT treat any character as a wildcard. To cover several addresses, a certificate MUST list each one in its own subjectAltName or issuerAltName entry.
sections.eli5: To check two addresses match, tidy up the website part the same way, then compare them letter by letter. The first half is never changed, so a capital letter is a different letter.

sections.title: Name Constraints in Path Validation
sections.content:
This section updates Section 4.2.1.10 of RFC 5280 so that rfc822Name name constraints also apply to SmtpUTF8Mailbox names. Both forms are the same underlying email namespace, so an existing CA restricted to certain domains stays restricted. RFC 9549 makes the matching change to RFC 5280, and constraints that name a particular mailbox (with a Local-part) SHOULD NOT be used.

For a constraint check, the Local-part and the @ are stripped, leaving the domain. If the constraint domain starts with a ., the end of the name's domain must match it octet for octet, including the dot. Otherwise the entire domain must match.

CAs that issue CA certificates with email name constraints MUST use rfc822Name only, with IDNA2008 names and non-ASCII domains as A-labels.
sections.eli5: A school-district certificate may only vouch for addresses at certain websites. The rule is checked on the website part, so both old and new kinds of address are held to the same limits.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The usual considerations of RFC 5280 apply, plus a new one: allowing non-ASCII characters in the Local-part brings the risk of visually similar or identical characters used to deceive a recipient.

A string of user-perceived characters can also be encoded in several Unicode ways, and RFC 6531 does not mandate a normalization form. To limit attacks that exploit this, the RFC requires octet-for-octet comparison of the Local-part. It admits that binary comparison may raise interoperability problems when the mail system and the CA use different encodings.
sections.eli5: Some letters from different alphabets look identical, so a trickster could fake an address. Comparing exact bytes helps, but it can also reject addresses that only differ in how they were typed.

sections.title: Differences from RFC 8398
sections.content:
There are three major changes from RFC 8398:

  • Domain labels in mail addresses are always encoded as LDH labels, using A-labels and never U-labels.
  • The matching algorithm now accepts only domain labels in A-label form.
  • The processing of rfc822Name name constraints likewise accepts only A-label domain labels.

IANA updated the references for the id-mod-lamps-eai-addresses-2016 module and the SmtpUTF8Mailbox otherName to point to this document.
sections.eli5: The older version let websites be written two ways. This version picks just one, which makes checking easier.
